Psychiatric Symptoms from Medical Illness or Medication

medication-induced psychosis · glucocorticoids · Cushing syndrome · delirium versus psychosis · medical workup before a primary diagnosisDid a drug or a disease start this, and is attention intact?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Rule out a drug or a medical illness before diagnosing a primary psychiatric disorder.

Three labels:

  • Medication-induced psychotic disorder: delusions or hallucinations that begin with a new medication
  • Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition: history, examination or laboratory evidence of a disease that directly causes the psychosis; they begin and end together
  • Delirium: fluctuating attention and disorientation; psychotic features, if present, are secondary

High-dose glucocorticoids may cause psychosis, typically in the first week but at any time, and also mania or depression.

Cushing syndrome often brings low or labile mood, anxiety, irritability, poor sleep, memory problems and fatigue, and can be mistaken for a primary psychiatric disorder.

Diagnosis
Defining features Medication-induced – acute delusions or hallucinations temporally linked to a new medication · Due to another medical condition – a disease known to cause psychosis (eg, central nervous system tumor, stroke, endocrine or autoimmune disorder), beginning and ending with it · Delirium – fluctuating cognition with poor attention and disorientation · Favors a primary psychosis – onset before 40, a prodrome, auditory (not visual, gustatory or tactile) hallucinations, family history of psychotic illness
Management and treatment
By cause Severe glucocorticoid psychosis or mania – first taper the dose toward under 40 mg/day of prednisone or the lowest dose possible, avoiding an aggressive taper (withdrawal risk); if the dose cannot be reduced, low-dose antipsychotics have resolved symptoms in case reports; lithium has been described for prevention, with more side effects · Due to a medical condition – treat the condition; some patients also need treatment for the psychosis itself · Cushing features with depression or anxiety – test for hypercortisolism before starting an antidepressant; exclude exogenous glucocorticoids first, the most common cause
Practice
  1. 64-year-old woman, day 10 of prednisone 60 mg daily for giant cell arteritis for 2 days sure neighbors poison her water; hears them plotting no psychiatric history or drug use alert, attentive, oriented · T 36.9 °C · examination otherwise normal → Medication-induced psychotic disorder → new delusions and hallucinations during high-dose prednisone (typical in the first week but possible at any time), with attention and orientation intact; delirium centers on fluctuating attention and disorientation, and brief psychotic disorder is excluded when a medication better explains the symptoms
  2. 57-year-old woman, 3 weeks of believing neighbors spy on her first psychiatric symptoms ever; no family history new trouble finding words; right hand clumsy alert and oriented · BP 138/84 mm Hg · toxicology, chemistry and thyroid tests normal → Brain MRI → onset after 40 with a speech and motor deficit points to a structural cause such as a stroke: image the brain before starting risperidone for a presumed primary psychosis; electroencephalography is for suspected seizure activity
  3. 78-year-old man on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for a lung flare since yesterday picks at the air, calls the nurse by his wife's name clear at noon, muddled by evening cannot name months backward · oriented to person only · T 37.2 °C → Delirium → fluctuating attention with disorientation is the core of delirium, and psychotic features may appear secondarily; here attention and orientation fail, whereas an alert, oriented patient makes delirium less likely; brief psychotic disorder is excluded when a medication or medical illness better explains the symptoms
  4. 36-year-old man, 3 months of panic attacks and poor sleep facial flushing; bruises easily; trouble rising from a chair uses no steroid pills, inhalers or creams BP 150/96 mm Hg · wide purple striae on the flanks · fasting glucose 128 mg/dL → 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test → panic attacks and insomnia with facial flushing, easy bruising, wide violaceous striae, proximal weakness, hypertension and high glucose suggest Cushing syndrome once exogenous glucocorticoids are excluded; rule out the medical cause before treating with sertraline, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor). Insulin-like growth factor 1 screens for acromegaly, which enlarges the jaw, hands and feet. The first test is chosen by suitability: late-night salivary cortisol may not suit variable bedtimes, and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol is also accepted
  5. 52-year-old man, day 6 of prednisone 60 mg daily for colitis no sleep for 3 nights; spent his savings says he can cure cancer; no psychiatric history; bowels improving alert and oriented · neurologic examination normal · HR 88/min · T 36.8 °C → Taper the prednisone dose → severe glucocorticoid-induced mania: dose reduction comes first, toward under 40 mg/day of prednisone or the lowest dose possible while the colitis allows; lithium has been described for prevention and has more side effects, and imaging is for a focal or cognitive finding
  6. 19-year-old man, 2 months of paranoia and irritability; grades falling slurred speech and an unsteady gait no drug use; urine toxicology negative T 36.7 °C · alanine aminotransferase 112 U/L · thyroid tests normal → Serum ceruloplasmin → psychosis with dysarthria, ataxia and abnormal liver tests points to Wilson disease: serum ceruloplasmin, with 24-hour urinary copper, before starting risperidone; a heavy metal screen is for cognitive deficits, ataxia, choreoathetosis and polyneuropathy, and dysarthria with abnormal liver tests is the Wilson pattern
Pairs with Psychosis: no drug or medical cause, then time it. Delirium: is attention fluctuating? Major Depressive Disorder: criteria met with no medical cause.
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychiatric disorder, ask what started before the symptoms: a drug, a dose, or a disease.
